params.question: A patient who has completed successful treatment for tuberculosis will immediately test negative on PCR.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: That statement is false. PCR detects DNA regardless of organism viability. A successfully treated TB patient may remain PCR-positive for weeks because dead mycobacterial DNA persists in the specimen. Always correlate molecular results with clinical response and culture.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. PCR amplifies nucleic acid from both living and dead organisms. After successful TB treatment, dead mycobacterial DNA can persist in specimens for weeks, keeping the result positive. Clinical improvement and culture negativity are needed to confirm cure.

params.question: A district hospital suspects Chlamydia trachomatis as the cause of a patient's urethritis. Standard bacterial culture yields no growth. Based on the test selection principles discussed, which investigation is most appropriate?

answers.text: Repeat culture on MacConkey agar with prolonged incubation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism and cannot grow on standard bacteriological media such as MacConkey agar, regardless of incubation time.

answers.text: Nucleic acid amplification test (PCR) for Chlamydia trachomatis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular pathogen that cannot grow on standard culture media. PCR detects its genetic material directly and is the recommended diagnostic method.

answers.text: Serum Widal test to detect cross-reacting antibodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Widal test detects antibodies against Salmonella Typhi, not Chlamydia. It has no role in diagnosing chlamydial urethritis.
Ziehl-Neelsen staining identifies acid-fast bacilli (primarily Mycobacterium species). Chlamydia is neither acid-fast nor visible on this stain.

overallFeedback.feedback: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism that cannot be cultured on standard bacteriological media. When pathogen biology precludes conventional culture, PCR or serology becomes the mandatory alternative.

Correct. Obligate intracellular organisms like Chlamydia and Rickettsia cannot grow on standard media, making PCR or serology mandatory — a key application of the pathogen biology factor in test selection.

params.question: In the epidemiological triad discussed in this session, disease emerges when the balance shifts in favour of the agent. Which set of factors constitutes the 'host' component of this triad?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are properties of the agent, not the host. The agent component describes the organism's inherent capacity to cause disease.
Correct. The host component includes factors that determine individual susceptibility — age, immune status, nutritional state, and comorbid conditions.
These are environmental factors, not host factors. The environment component describes external conditions that facilitate or hinder disease transmission.

answers.text: Reservoir, portal of exit, and route of transmission

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are elements of the chain of transmission, a separate framework from the epidemiological triad. The chain describes how infection moves from source to susceptible host.

overallFeedback.feedback: The host component includes factors affecting individual susceptibility: age, immune status, nutrition, and comorbidities. Remember to distinguish the triad (agent, host, environment) from the chain of transmission (reservoir, portal of exit, route, susceptible host).

Correct. The host component — age, immune status, nutrition, and comorbidities — determines individual susceptibility. Disease occurs when agent, host, and environmental factors align in favour of the pathogen.

params.question: A laboratory technician routinely applies stricter biosafety precautions to specimens labelled 'HIV-positive' while using standard precautions for unlabelled specimens. This practice is:

answers.text: Appropriate, because HIV carries a higher transmission risk than most pathogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Universal precautions exist because any specimen may carry blood-borne pathogens, including unlabelled ones. Differential handling creates a false sense of safety and is a form of discrimination.

answers.text: Discriminatory and irrational, because any specimen can carry blood-borne pathogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Universal precautions must apply equally to every specimen. Singling out HIV-labelled samples implies unlabelled specimens are safe — which is irrational — and stigmatises patients whose diagnosis is known.

answers.text: Required under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The HIV Act, 2017 protects patient confidentiality and prohibits discrimination. It does not mandate stricter precautions for labelled specimens — differential handling would contravene its anti-discrimination provisions.

answers.text: Acceptable if the technician has not received hepatitis B vaccination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vaccination status does not justify differential specimen handling. Universal precautions apply regardless of the handler's immunisation history.

overallFeedback.feedback: Universal precautions must be applied uniformly to every specimen. Applying stricter measures only to HIV-labelled samples is discriminatory and irrational — any specimen can carry blood-borne pathogens.

Exactly right. Universal precautions apply equally to all specimens. Differential handling is both discriminatory and a biosafety failure, since unlabelled specimens may carry the same blood-borne pathogens.
